cards.heading: Anatomy of a route
cards.body: Every line in 'show ip route' answers four questions: how the route was learned (the code), which destination prefix it covers, how trustworthy and how good it is [administrative distance/metric], and where to send the packet (next hop or exit interface). For a dynamic route the timer (00:03:11) shows how long ago it was learned or last updated; static and connected routes don't have one. A line such as '10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 4 subnets, 3 masks' is a heading, not a route: four routes inside 10.0.0.0/8 follow, using three prefix lengths. 'show ip route ospf' filters the table to OSPF routes only.
cards.example:
O    172.16.0.0/16 [110/20] via 10.0.0.2, 00:03:11, Gi0/0
│    │              │   │       └ next hop
│    │              │   └ metric (OSPF cost)
│    │              └ administrative distance
│    └ destination prefix
└ code: O = OSPF

cards.heading: Connected and local routes
cards.body: When an interface has an IP address and is up/up, the router adds two routes by itself: C for the connected subnet and L, a /32 for its own address on that interface. Both have administrative distance 0.
cards.example:
C    10.0.0.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L    10.0.0.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0

cards.heading: Longest prefix match
cards.body: To forward a packet the router looks at every route whose prefix contains the destination and uses the most specific one, the longest prefix. AD and metric play no part here; they were already used to decide which routes got into the table.

cards.heading: Administrative distance
cards.body: If two sources offer the same prefix and length, only one is installed: the one with the lowest administrative distance. Metrics are compared only between routes from the same protocol. A floating static route gets a deliberately high AD so it's used only as a backup. Fuller list: internal EIGRP 90, external EIGRP 170, iBGP 200, and 255 means never trusted, so a route with AD 255 is never installed. A floating static route only wins if its AD is lower than the other source: at AD 200 it stays out while an external EIGRP route (170) exists. If the installed route disappears, the next-best source's route is installed instead.
cards.example:
Connected 0   Static 1   eBGP 20   EIGRP 90
OSPF 110      RIP 120    iBGP 200
ip route 10.9.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.0.0.6 130   ← floating static
cards.mnemonic:
Trust goes from what you can see to what you hear second-hand. Connected is 0 (you can see it), Static is 1 (you typed it), eBGP is 20.
Then the inside protocols: EIGRP 90 sits just under 100, and OSPF 110 and RIP 120 just over, ten apart, with old RIP trusted least.
Routes heard second-hand are high: external EIGRP 170, iBGP 200. And 255 means never.

cards.heading: The default route
cards.body: 0.0.0.0/0 matches every destination but is the least specific route, so it's used only when nothing else matches. It shows up as the 'gateway of last resort'. With no default route, a packet that matches nothing is dropped. The * marks a candidate default route; its next hop becomes the gateway of last resort. 'Gateway of last resort is not set' means there's no default route. OSPF advertises a default as O*E2: OSPF, external type 2, candidate default.

cards.heading: No match, TTL and equal-cost paths
cards.body: If nothing matches and there's no default route, the router drops the packet and sends ICMP destination unreachable to the source. Every router that forwards a packet lowers its TTL by one; at zero it drops the packet and sends ICMP time exceeded, which is how traceroute maps a path. Two routes to the same prefix from the same protocol with equal best metric are both installed, and traffic is shared between them (ECMP). OSPF installs up to 4 equal-cost paths by default ('maximum-paths' under router ospf). With unequal costs, only the lowest-cost path goes in.

cards.heading: Codes, metrics and the IPv6 table
cards.body: Codes: C connected, L local, S static, D EIGRP (from DUAL), O OSPF, R RIP; C, L and S aren't learned from a dynamic protocol. Each protocol has its own metric: OSPF uses cost (from interface bandwidth), RIP hop count, and EIGRP a composite of bandwidth and delay. In 'show ipv6 route' the local route for each address is a /128, and routes learned from a routing protocol use the neighbour's link-local address (FE80::...) plus the exit interface as the next hop. 'show ip route 10.5.5.5' shows the entry that matches one address: 'from 2.2.2.2' is the advertising router's ID and 'via' the next hop; one descriptor block means one path.
cards.example:
O   2001:DB8:2::/64 [110/2]
     via FE80::2, GigabitEthernet0/1
L   2001:DB8:1::1/128 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/0, receive
cards.mnemonic:
Most codes are first letters: C connected, L local, S static, O OSPF, R RIP, B BGP.
The odd one is EIGRP, which is D: E was already taken by the older EGP protocol. Remember D for DUAL, EIGRP's algorithm.
L is always a single address (/32 or /128): the router's own.

cards.heading: How the packet is actually forwarded
cards.body: A route with only a next hop needs a recursive lookup: the router looks up the next-hop address itself, normally matching a connected route, to find the exit interface. A packet for one of the router's own addresses matches the local /32 route, so the router processes it instead of forwarding it. When forwarding, IP addresses stay end-to-end (without NAT); the router builds a new layer 2 frame with its own MAC as the source and the next hop's MAC (found with ARP) as the destination, and decrements the TTL. By default Cisco routers use Cisco Express Forwarding (CEF): it precomputes a forwarding information base (FIB) from the routing table's best routes and an adjacency table of layer 2 rewrite information for each next hop.
